claims.text: The bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimen has typical defect concentrations.
The bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimen has a measured oxygen impurity level of approximately 1 wt.%.
A model combining atomistic simulations with machine-learning corrections can incorporate defect-bearing and oxygen-containing calibration data.
Quantum and defect scattering dominate electrical transport in the 0–200 K regime.
Phonon scattering is significant in the 300–1200 K regime.
Variations in defect density mediate electron and phonon scattering in bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen impurity sites mediate electron and phonon scattering in bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
Explicitly modeling lattice imperfections and oxygen impurities better captures the real transport-scattering processes.
Better representation of scattering processes will improve electrical-conductivity predictions at both low and high temperatures.
The hybrid defect-tolerant model will predict conductivity more accurately across 0–200 K than standard perfect-crystal analytical models.
The hybrid defect-tolerant model will predict conductivity more accurately across 300–1200 K than standard perfect-crystal analytical models.
High-temperature predictions for specimens containing about 1 wt.% oxygen will improve substantially.
Existing analytical conductivity models assume defect-free crystals.
Existing defect-free analytical models show significant deviations from measured conductivity, especially when oxygen impurities are present.
The expected accuracy advantage is limited to systems similar to bulk HfNbTaTiZr with oxygen levels near 1 wt.%.
The model may not generalize to alloys with substantially different defect chemistry or higher impurity concentrations.
